name: Felix Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit walls and fire doors on a hospital refurbishment where clinics keep running beside us. I have a vocational trade certificate and nine years with this contractor, so I know the site rhythms. A door that closes flush without waking the whole corridor is a good day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Design changes after we board a wall, and the noise restrictions when a clinic is open. My partner Ines works in a school kitchen; we have two children in school and a mortgage. I try an AI explanation tool now and then, but I trust the measured opening more than its answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the walls and doors still need people to fit them. A bit less office paperwork would be welcome. A neat plan is not the same thing as a square door frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines and I have more than six months saved and my building-site pay is good. The mortgage is still there, and we have two children in school, but there are plenty of contractors close enough for me to change sites if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with the hospital refurbishment and keep hanging doors against the measured openings. I would use the simple AI explanation tool I already try now and then for paperwork, then check the actual specification with the site manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The mortgage is a responsibility, not a fire to put out every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is difficult about the hospital site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic runs beside our work, so one noisy cut at the wrong hour stops a whole appointment room. I check the day’s access note before opening a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ines and I already set aside money each pay day, and a plateau would not change that amount or the children’s school costs.

say: I would tell the crew **doors and walls** still need careful hands on building sites.
I would welcome a small **paperwork saving** without trusting an unchecked plan.
think: Our **savings and pay** keep the mortgage manageable alongside two school-age children.
Plenty of **nearby contractors** give me options if this site finishes.
do: Keep fitting **hospital fire doors** to measured openings.
Use the existing **AI paperwork helper** occasionally and verify specifications with the site manager.
S0.quote: A neat plan is not the same thing as a square door frame.
fieldNote: His housing and childcare costs are real, but **strong savings** and local work support calm.
His occasional AI use is **already routine**, so this is continuation rather than new learning.

steps.text: Keep fitting hospital fire doors and verifying measurements on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can order materials faster, but the builders should check whether the delivery actually fits the room. I would bring the late design changes to our union site meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My carpentry hours should hold for now; robots come more slowly to this work. I could still lose overtime if software makes the contractor price every job tighter, though Ines’s school kitchen wage and our savings give the household room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare my next three pay slips with the building rota. If overtime falls, we would delay the new garden shed, and I would ask the union meeting for a written rule on who approves AI-generated cut lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my hours, even though I can take another local site. I want the crew to have a say before targets change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake in a cut list worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cabinet panel cut for the drawing rather than the wall that is actually there. The carpenter gets blamed when an AI cut list leaves a gap beside a hospital cabinet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shed delay hurt the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They can keep playing in the garden; the shed is for my tools. We would keep paying the mortgage and school expenses first.

say: I would ask builders to check **AI cut lists** against actual rooms.
I would take late design changes to the **union site meeting** before new targets become routine.
think: My **carpentry work** continues, but tighter pricing could reduce paid overtime.
Our **second wage** and savings give room, yet a smaller pay packet would affect plans.
do: Compare three **pay slips** with the building rota for lost overtime.
Delay the **garden shed** if overtime falls.
Raise an **approval rule** for AI cut lists at the next union site meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about realistically thinner overtime, with nearby sites as a backup.
S1.quote: The carpenter gets blamed when an AI cut list leaves a gap beside a hospital cabinet.
fieldNote: His union action concerns a concrete **cut-list approval** and crew accountability.
The garden shed is a conditional **spending cut**, while mortgage and school costs remain protected.

steps.text: Delay the garden tool shed if paid overtime falls
Raise AI cut-list approval at the next union site meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 may write the site plans, but nobody has a robot fitting doors until around 2031. We should be checking real work, not a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could change quickly and shorten our schedules before capable robots arrive. I could lose carpentry days when robots finally fit the frames, but the mortgage is not in danger tomorrow because we have savings and Ines still earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the hospital site while it has shifts and make a list of local refurbishment contractors with open vacancies. If two monthly rosters cut my paid days, I would apply for a posted role at comparable pay before leaving my current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours from 2031 onward. I can move between sites. My children need a predictable week, even if I can change building sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the savings on a new trade course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from a headline alone. I would first ask whether a course leads to a posted paid role and whether the contractor offers paid time to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines after a bad roster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Ines, my partner, the paid days and the vacancy list. We would decide together whether an offer covers the mortgage and school costs.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** changes plans before capable robots reach door fitting around 2031.
I would demand **site evidence** before contractors use robots to cut carpentry crews.
think: A robot could cut my **paid days** while the mortgage and school bills continue.
Our **savings**, Ines’s wage and local contractors keep us from an immediate crisis.
do: Keep **hospital refurbishment** shifts while they are paid.
Apply to **posted local jobs** after two reduced rosters, leaving only for comparable pay.
feel: **Anxious** about future days, with a workable local search plan.
S2.quote: My children need a predictable week, even if I can change building sites.
fieldNote: He separates the **2028 planning change** from the roughly three-year delay for capable robots.
His job search requires **two reduced rosters** and an offer protecting mortgage and school expenses.

steps.text: Keep hospital carpentry shifts while paid work continues
Apply to posted local carpentry jobs after two reduced rosters for comparable pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to test machines on a crooked old building, not just a new empty room. A robot fitting doors in 2034 should be checked against the fire rules we follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be forty eight when thinking AI reaches 2031 and fifty one at the robot date. That is too young to stop work, but with a lead time I could learn a new site role if the employer paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep hanging doors this year. If the contractor posts a paid building-robot maintenance place, I would take the training on paid time and apply; otherwise I would stay with carpentry and watch the local vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, edging anxious if there are fewer doors for human fitters. A funded path would give me something solid to work toward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a vacancy. We could afford the fee, but I will not use mortgage money for a certificate with no paid job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the door closes properly after the wall settles and whether a worker can stop the machine. An empty showroom tells us little about a fire door in an old hospital.

say: I would test **2034 fitting robots** on crooked older buildings and fire doors.
I would ask for a **worker stop control** before the contractor relies on a machine.
think: I still need decades of **paid work** beyond the thinking AI and robot dates.
A funded **maintenance role** could make change manageable if the contractor posts one.
do: Complete **paid maintenance training** and apply only if a real contractor vacancy is posted.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible loss of fitting work, with a conditional new route.
S3.quote: An empty showroom tells us little about a fire door in an old hospital.
fieldNote: His training plan is tied to a **posted paid vacancy** and paid time.
A strong cushion helps, but age forty three means **many working years** remain after 2034.

steps.text: Keep hospital door fitting shifts this year
Complete paid building-robot maintenance training only if a contractor posts a paid vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices that a decade is time to learn the trade properly and argue for fair retraining. Thinking AI in 2036 changes drawings first; robots that fit doors arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I would be fifty six, still needing earnings for the mortgage and what comes after it. I can plan ahead with our savings, but I cannot tell the children that carpentry pay will last unchanged forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the hospital work during 2026 and add a small extra payment to the mortgage from each wage if Ines and I confirm school costs stay covered. In the first year after 2036 I would review actual site hours before choosing new training, and in 2039 I would seek posted work if fitting hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan, uneasy about what our children will see. A decade lets us save from real wages rather than guess at prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps fifty from each pay packet, but only after we check the children’s costs and the emergency reserve. I do not want to win a mortgage race and lose the family buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I will still be in my fifties when the capable robots come; my plan is to keep paid work in building trades if possible.

say: I would seek **fair retraining** while apprentices still get hands-on carpentry years.
I would explain the **2036/2039 gap** between smart plans and capable fitting robots.
think: I will still need **paid work** when robots reach construction around 2039.
Our **savings** let us prepare without assuming any guaranteed future wage.
do: Keep **2026 hospital work** and pay extra mortgage principal if school costs stay covered.
Review **2036 site hours** before choosing training or applying for posted 2039 work.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-run work while able to plan from a strong cushion.
S4.quote: I do not want to win a mortgage race and lose the family buffer.
fieldNote: The extra debt payment is genuine **new cushion building**, conditional on school costs and reserve.
He separates **2026 work** from later information gathering and a conditional job search.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal from wages only if school costs and reserves allow
Review actual site hours after 2036 before choosing new training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could cut fitting days by 2031 while our children and mortgage still need a wage. Posted local jobs with comparable pay and paid training for a real role would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a fire door after a robot fits it. A tidy drawing will not hold smoke back if the gap is wrong.

headlineQuote: A tidy drawing will not hold smoke back if the gap is wrong.
portrait: **Felix**, 43, is an experienced hospital-site fitter with a trade certificate, higher pay, strong savings and many nearby contractors.
He and Ines support **two school-age children** and a mortgage, giving him reason to protect predictable paid days.
He uses **AI occasionally**, waits for proven tools and raises practical design and safety issues at union meetings.
The **2028 case** worries him because robots could reach door fitting in 2031, long before his working life ends.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his carpentry days once capable robots reach building sites around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Comparable local jobs** and paid training linked to a posted role would help the family plan.
